lines: The message arrived in the middle of a Tuesday, which is how the biggest things always arrive.
Dr. Abena Osei was eating cold jollof at her desk when the array in Chile flagged an anomaly in the data from Kepler-442b: a pulse, regular, every eleven seconds, for forty-one minutes.
She sent it to the team.
Abena played the pulse through a pair of old headphones and realised what had been bothering her.
A particular, familiar, human rhythm: the three-two clave her grandfather used to tap on the dashboard of his taxi.
Twelve hundred light years away, nobody could have heard it from us.
Whatever was out there had arrived at the same heartbeat by itself.
And it was not answering with mathematics, or warnings, or demands.
It was simply keeping time, the way you do with a stranger at a party when a song comes on that you both love, and you tap along, and neither of you says a word.
